ddx.step1_summary:
• Chief complaint: “Blinding” headache for the past 3 days.
• Symptoms:
  – Onset/Duration: Sudden onset upon waking; persistent for 3 days.
  – Location: Diffuse but worst over right eye.
  – Character/Severity: Constant, 8/10 at worst, decreases to 5/10 with ibuprofen but never fully resolves.
  – Associated features: Photophobia, transient “shooting lights” / visual disturbance, mild nausea (no vomiting), no focal neurologic deficits (numbness, weakness, speech changes), no fever, no sinus/respiratory symptoms.
  – Aggravating: Bright light, sudden standing/head movement.
  – Alleviating: Partial relief with ibuprofen, able to sleep (headache does not wake her at night).
• Past medical history: Essentially none; vague childhood “pain” that resolved.
• Medications/Allergies:
  – Combined oral contraceptive pill (started 1 yr ago; exact brand not specified).
  – PRN ibuprofen; no other drugs.
  – No known drug or other allergies.
• Family history: Mother suffers from migraines with vomiting.
• Social history: Lives alone, works from home. Non-smoker. Alcohol ~3 drinks once weekly. No recreational drugs. No recent travel.
• Vital signs / exam findings: None performed yet (tele-visit only). Patient afebrile by history; last BP check 1 yr ago “normal.”
• Labs/imaging: None obtained/mentioned.

V: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST): Young female on estrogen-containing OCP with new severe headache; may worsen with positional changes.
Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Sudden severe headache described as ‘blinding’; however less classically “thunderclap.”
I: Viral or aseptic meningitis: Persistent headache with photophobia; no fever or meningismus but still possible.
Sinusitis (frontal/ethmoidal): Facial pressure described previously; current lack of congestion argues against but worth noting.
N: Intracranial mass/brain tumor: Progressive persistent headache with visual disturbance; needs exclusion despite short duration.
D: Tension-type headache: Constant pressure-like pain, worsened by stress/work, partially relieved by NSAIDs.
I2: OCP-related migraine (medication-induced): Estrogen can trigger de-novo migraine with aura.
C: Chiari I malformation: Occipital/positional headaches that may worsen with Valsalva or sudden movement.
A: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH): Young woman, OCP use, visual phenomena; needs fundoscopic exam for papilledema.
T: Post-traumatic headache: No head injury reported—low likelihood.
E: Primary migraine with aura: Photophobia, visual ‘shooting lights’, unilateral predominance, family history; classic presentation.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: New unilateral severe headache with photophobia and visual phenomena, family history of classic migraine, partial ibuprofen response, absence of red-flag neurologic signs.
Risk factors (female, estrogen-containing OCP), acute persistent headache, positional worsening, not fully relieved by analgesics; potentially serious and easily missed.
Young woman, OCP use, visual symptoms; requires optic-disc exam. However headache not worse lying down and no diplopia, so less classic.
Diffuse constant headache partially relieved with NSAID; but severity (8/10), photophobia, and visual aura make primary tension headache less likely.
Sudden severe onset could fit, but persistence without peak ‘worst ever’ thunderclap, no neck stiffness, vomiting, or neurologic deficit lowers probability.

supporting_evidence: Photophobia and avoidance of bright lights.
Previous mild headaches responsive to NSAIDs, now worse—typical evolution.
opposing_evidence: First prolonged episode lasting >72 h (status migrainosus—but still migraine spectrum).
Lack of classic pulsatile description or vomiting.

supporting_evidence: New severe persistent headache unrelieved by analgesics.
opposing_evidence: No focal neurologic deficits, seizures, or papilledema reported.
Onset not clearly progressive over days to weeks as often seen.

supporting_evidence: Female of child-bearing age, on OCP.
Headache present on waking (can occur with raised ICP).
opposing_evidence: No documented papilledema or transient visual obscurations.
Headache reportedly worse on standing rather than lying down.
No mention of pulsatile tinnitus or diplopia.

supporting_evidence: Diffuse bilateral pressure-like pain described historically.
Stress/working from home could be contributing.
opposing_evidence: High severity (8/10) atypical for tension HA.
Photophobia and visual aura not features of tension headache.

supporting_evidence: Sudden onset severe headache described as ‘blinding’.
Positional exacerbation possible with raised ICP.
opposing_evidence: Not described as ‘worst ever’ thunderclap; persists without initial peak then improvement.
No meningismus, vomiting, or neurologic deficit.
Able to sleep; pain decreases to 5/10 with NSAID.
